questions.enonce_markdown:
Evaluate the temptations of Jesus and bring out their relevance.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Luke 4:1-13 tells how Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit and led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days, was tempted by the devil. The story follows his baptism, where he was declared God's Son (3:22), and comes before his public ministry.

**1. The three temptations in Luke.** (a) To turn a stone into bread, when he was hungry. Jesus answers from Deuteronomy: "One does not live by bread alone." (b) To receive the authority and glory of all the kingdoms of the world, if he would worship the devil. Jesus answers: "Worship the Lord your God, and serve only him." (c) To throw himself down from the pinnacle of the Temple in Jerusalem, trusting God's angels to protect him, with the devil quoting Psalm 91. Jesus answers: "Do not put the Lord your God to the test." Luke ends in Jerusalem, where his story will end, and says the devil left him "until an opportune time" (4:13).

**2. Evaluation.** The tests concern Jesus' identity as Son of God: "If you are the Son of God." They tempt him to use his power for himself, to gain power by a shortcut without the cross, and to demand a spectacular sign of God's protection. In each case Jesus chooses obedience to God and trust in Scripture. Where Israel failed in the wilderness for forty years, Jesus, in forty days, shows himself the faithful Son.

**3. Relevance to the ministry of Jesus.** The testing defines the kind of Messiah he will be: not a provider of bread by magic, not a political ruler, not a wonder-worker for show. It prepares for later pressures, for example Peter's rejection of the cross (9:22) and the garden of Gethsemane, where he tells his disciples to pray that they may not come into temptation (22:40-46).

**4. Relevance to believers.** Christians see Jesus as sharing human testing (compare Hebrews 4:15) and as a model for resisting it: knowing and using the word of God, putting God before material needs, refusing to compromise for power, and not presuming on God. The three temptations correspond to contemporary pressures: materialism and consumerism, the love of power and position, and religious showiness.

**Conclusion.** The temptations show Jesus' obedience as Son and clarify the nature of his mission. For believers they remain a pattern of how to meet temptation with dependence on God.
